The original GP 2 compiler has been significantly improved by incorporating the OpenCL 1.2 front end, which has been developed using the GP 2 front end toolkit. This enhancement enables GP 2 to generate high-performance code for a variety of hardware accelerators, including GPUs, FPGAs, and many-core processors, by leveraging an existing compiler such as LLVM. The new enhanced compiler is readily available for use and can be easily extended to support additional languages and hardware platforms.

To improve the efficiency of attribute extraction in e-commerce, a new method called UASRC-L is proposed. This model utilizes a unified data structure and contrastive learning to organize and learn from a vast amount of unstructured product information. By employing a BERT-based text encoder and a matrix decomposition decoder, UASRC-L can effectively represent and generate accurate attribute information from diverse input formats. A specially designed attribute mask attention mechanism further enhances the extraction of missing attributes. Experimental results demonstrate that UASRC-L achieves high-quality attribute completion and extraction, outperforming existing methods in terms of F1-score and macro-F1-score. Additionally, UASRC-L's ability to handle unstructured information makes it a versatile and powerful tool for various NLP tasks.

A finite quotient network is defined as a quotient of a network $\Lambda$ under a group $G$, where the vertex set of the quotient retains the property of $G$-transitivity. Recently, researchers have focused on identifying infinite collections of network structures that possess star normal properties. This paper introduces a new infinite family of star normal quotient networks of twisted wreath properties, based on a network constructed from a primitive solvable type and its associated twisted product group. The existence of these star normal properties is verified through the development of a suitable section system. This work extends previous findings by expanding the range of star normal network structures with properties such as twisted wreath properties and multiple transitivity. The findings are established via the development of a specific section system and demonstrate the potential for further exploration in this area of study.

For categorical data with many dimensions, effective feature selection is crucial for reducing complexity and improving model interpretability. Although some group-based methods have been developed, they often struggle with scalability when dealing with high-dimensional data sets. To address this, we investigated the Group Lasso method, which can handle block-structured data, but found that it can be sensitive to data partitioning. We propose an enhancement to this method by incorporating an auto-encoder to create a more optimal block structure. We evaluated our approach using both simulated and real-world data sets, and the results demonstrate that it can effectively select relevant features and produce models that are easier to understand.

Recent advancements in vision models have been fueled by the success of ResNet, a structured approach that combines vision features with infused insights to boost performance on various tasks. In this paper, we propose a novel, structured method for text-based understanding called SKILL (Structured Insight Infusion for Language Models). By integrating insights from large language models with infused insights into a structured framework, we achieve superior performance on multiple text-based tasks. Our experiments demonstrate that SKILL outperforms existing methods on eight text-based tasks, including natural language inference, multi-task dialogue understanding, and natural language inference. Our code is available at https://github.com/AllenAI/Structured-Insight-Infusion-for-Extensive-LangModels.

This paper proposes a novel nonlocal diffusion model that relies on short-range interactions, and demonstrates in theoretical analysis that as the range of these interactions increases, the model converges to a classical local diffusion model described by a second-order elliptic equation with an $L^\infty$ coefficient. Conversely, this model exhibits distinct scaling properties and demonstrates optimal long-range interaction scaling in a nontrivial manner that bridges two distinct regimes.

When viewing the world from a single vantage point, a panoramic image replicates this view by combining multiple overlapping pictures. Typically, the camera is positioned at eye level, and the pictures are divided into three sections: upper, lower, and central. The upper and lower sections are often skewed, whereas the central section is more aligned. This occurs because the human eye naturally focuses on objects at eye level, and as a result, the central section of the image is less distorted. This characteristic can be utilized to create a panoramic image that is optimally aligned, with the minimum number of source pictures required. A common approach to achieving this involves dividing the image into separate sections and applying different processing techniques to each. In this research, a novel approach is proposed that leverages the natural preference for eye-level viewing to create a panoramic image that is both efficient and visually appealing. The proposed approach is tested against existing methods, and the results indicate that it outperforms them in terms of both accuracy and efficiency.

This paper delves into the local behavior of an Eisenstein series at a specific singular point in a given group, where the series is constructed from a specific type of unramified representation. The analysis involves the use of two combinatorial tools, specifically reduced expressions and the Frenkel-Kac basis, to better understand the underlying structure of the series.

Neurodegenerative diseases, such as Parkinson's, pose a significant threat to human health and are among the leading causes of disability worldwide. As the global population ages, the incidence of these disorders is expected to rise, necessitating the development of accurate computational models to simulate their pathophysiology. Current computational models of Parkinson's are limited in their ability to accurately replicate the disease's progression and are often disconnected from experimental data. To address this gap, we have created a novel computational model of Parkinson's that is based on a deep understanding of the brain's physiology and incorporates data from non-human primate studies. Our model utilizes a biophysically accurate simulation of the primate brain, along with a detailed database of brain cell types and their metabolic processes, to simulate the disease's progression. By introducing mutations and cell death associated with Parkinson's, our model is able to replicate the disease's symptoms and pathology, including the loss of dopamine-producing neurons and the resulting motor symptoms. This computational model has the potential to accelerate the development of effective treatments for Parkinson's by allowing researchers to test new therapies in a controlled, simulated environment.

When rendering line-based connections on high-resolution computer maps, a phenomenon known as spatial anti-aliasing can cause unexpected jumps in the drawn paths. This issue arises due to the mapping of real-world coordinates to a limited screen display, and has significant implications for user experience and navigation. To address this problem, an innovative line rendering algorithm has been developed, which employs a variable pixel width to prevent the occurrence of space anti-aliasing. This approach has been integrated into an online mapping system, and the results demonstrate substantial improvements in rendering accuracy and user experience. Furthermore, the proposed solution is versatile and can be applied to a range of scenarios, including route planning and location marking. To further enhance the algorithm's efficiency, an optimized data structure has been proposed, which minimizes memory usage and processing time. This research contributes valuable insights to the fields of computer graphics and geographic information systems.

We utilized the KOOLS-IFU on the Seimei Telescope to conduct optical integral field unit observations of 9 ultra/luminous infrared galaxies located within 0.04 units of redshift. These targets were selected based on their strong CO emission, and kinematic analysis of their stellar components was performed using the code SKIDA. The results revealed that the stellar components of these galaxies exhibit typical rotation curves, with some showing characteristics of two-component rotation curves. Additionally, the code SKIDA was able to derive the stellar mass of these galaxies, and the mass-to-light ratios were found to be consistent with previous studies. However, the stellar masses of these galaxies are significantly lower than those predicted from their infrared luminosity, and this discrepancy is attributed to the underestimation of the stellar mass by the code SKIDA. This discrepancy is also observed in other samples of galaxies, and it is likely due to the code SKIDA's inability to accurately account for the effects of dust on the mass-to-light ratio.

This research paper introduces a new radial basis function, the transcendental rational exponential function, which possesses desirable mathematical properties such as the ability to model a wide range of behaviors and the capacity to maintain the shape of the data. The RBF exhibits excellent approximation capabilities and the ability to fit both smooth and non-smooth functions. The proposed TRE function is then employed in the development of a novel quasi-interpolation operator, which has the ability to preserve the form and accuracy of functions in the polynomial space, while also exhibiting high rates of convergence. Theoretical analysis and numerical experiments are conducted to demonstrate the high accuracy and efficiency of the interpolation scheme. The results indicate that the method is capable of accurately approximating functions with both smooth and non-smooth characteristics. The study is the first to examine the use of TRE functions in interpolation and numerical differentiation. The proposed operator exhibits the ability to preserve the form and accuracy of functions in the polynomial space, while also exhibiting high rates of convergence. The theoretical analysis and numerical experiments are conducted to demonstrate the high accuracy and efficiency of the interpolation scheme. The results indicate that the method is capable of accurately approximating functions with both smooth and non-smooth characteristics. This research paper introduces an innovative concept called Climate Categorization, which utilizes advanced imaging technology to automatically determine the climate type of a geographical area. The authors have created a comprehensive dataset encompassing 1000 km² of varied landscapes, featuring images from multiple locations with distinct climate types. To overcome the limitations of existing approaches, a new data augmentation technique has been developed, which employs a sophisticated method to enhance the dataset's diversity and accuracy. The study has also compared various neural network architectures to identify the most effective configuration for accurate climate categorization. The proposed method has demonstrated superior performance over traditional techniques, achieving a high level of precision and recall in predicting the climate type of a geographical area. The authors have made their dataset and code publicly available to facilitate further research and development in the field of climate categorization.

To enhance speech quality in noisy environments, deep learning-based end-to-end systems have been successfully applied in real-world scenarios. However, these models often struggle with training efficiency and speech quality preservation. To address these challenges, we propose a novel Dual-Path Convolutional Recurrent Network (DPCRN) that combines the strengths of convolutional neural networks and recurrent neural networks. This innovative architecture allows for long-term temporal modeling and efficient training through parallel data processing. Experimental results on the Voice Bank-DEMAND dataset demonstrate the superiority of our model over state-of-the-art methods in terms of mean opinion score and distortion factor. Furthermore, our model's reduced number of trainable parameters and faster training time make it a practical and efficient solution for speech enhancement tasks.

In various cosmological models, researchers have investigated how different theories and particle properties affect the sizes of dark matter structures at their expansion limits. To better understand this, a modified halo finder technique was developed to incorporate multiple theories and parameters into simulations based on $f(R)$ gravity and sterile neutrino dark matter. By running simulations with different Rodriguez-Merino parameters and fourth-order Riemann curvature constants, researchers were able to determine the impact of these factors on dark matter halos. The results indicate that higher R values lead to smaller halos, while more neutrino mass leads to larger turn-around radii. Additionally, a new equation of state was developed to predict the turn-around radii of dark matter halos, which can be used to determine the R value from observational data.

This research aims to develop a multi-fluid model for atmospheric circulation by first testing a simplified scenario. We simulate the Rayleigh-B\'{e}nard convection using a single-column model, which involves two non-reactive fluids with different thermal properties. The model's mass and thermal energy are conserved, and it is applied to an infinitely deep atmosphere. We compare the multi-fluid model's results with a single-fluid model under identical conditions. The study finds that when thermal diffusivity is low, the models produce similar convection velocities, but significant differences arise when thermal diffusivity is high. Furthermore, the rate of convection velocity in relation to thermal diffusivity varies between the single-fluid and multi-fluid models.

We examine a system of two independent atoms, each initially in a ground state, that are separately coupled to two distinct cavities. By applying a semi-classical field to one of the cavities, we transfer the atoms to their excited states. However, this process does not create genuine entanglement between the atoms. To achieve genuine entanglement, we then apply the following steps: first, we exchange the state of the atom in the stimulated cavity with that of the atom in the dark cavity through the interaction between the two cavities, described by the Jaynes-Cummings model. We demonstrate that this entanglement swapping process can be controlled by adjusting the exchange time. Our theoretical analysis is supported by numerical simulations taking into account the effects of decoherence.

The CMS experiment at the LHC is designed to investigate the medium created during heavy-ion collisions and to study the rare decay of the Higgs boson into muons. To accomplish these goals, an upgraded pixel detector system is necessary to enhance the tracking capabilities for both types of experiments. To reduce the complexity of the upgrade, a new production method for the detector components was implemented, resulting in a single type of sensor that caters to both goals. However, this approach has led to an increase in the number of faulty components, posing a challenge for the data analysis. This paper examines the reconstruction of a large set of detector components, known as blades, to identify and rectify errors in the manufacturing process. The analysis involves the use of machine learning techniques to improve the identification of faulty components, with the aim of achieving a precise reconstruction of each blade. The results of the examination demonstrate the effectiveness of the analysis in achieving a precise reconstruction of each blade, with a high level of accuracy.

Using a non-perturbative approach, specifically Lattice QCD, we have obtained the Kall\'en-Lehmann spectral density for the scalar SU(2) glueball. By applying a Lattice QCD determination of the glueball two-point correlation function, we derived the spectral density in a theory-independent manner. Our analysis reveals a distinct mass state at approximately 2.4 GeV, which we interpret as the lowest glueball resonance. Further analysis of resonance parameters shows that a small width, around 0.1 GeV, is required to accurately describe the ground state. Our study also provides initial evidence for continuum structure in the spectral density, although more lattice data is needed to fully explore this feature. Additionally, our research offers guidance for future lattice QCD studies of hadronic spectra using GLUE balls as a template.

Social sentiment analysis is an effective means of understanding public opinion on various topics, including political events, product launches, and natural disasters. This study introduces a novel sentiment classification approach that leverages Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks to accurately interpret public sentiment expressed on Twitter. By incorporating pre-trained word embeddings and utilizing the Twitter API, this research demonstrates the efficacy of LSTM networks in sentiment assessment. The proposed method achieves a high level of accuracy, reaching 90.5%, in classifying the training dataset.

A novel method has been developed to calculate entropy and thermodynamic volume for black holes in a non-linearly charged AdS spacetime. This method, referred to as the "shadow method," was derived based on the correspondence between a black hole and its "shadow" through the use of an effective Gauss Bonmian density. When applying this method using the non-linear AdS-RN metric, the results matched those obtained using the first law of black hole thermodynamics. However, the method gave different outcomes when the spacetime was linearly charged. Notably, the "shadow method" produced an extra term, specifically -r_+^2/r_c, which had no equivalent in the corresponding linear spacetime.

We examine the characteristics of quantum synchronization using mixed states and investigate its behavior in quantum damped harmonic oscillators through various density matrices. Our analysis focuses on how quantum synchronization is influenced by entanglement, as measured by the partial transpose and Slant entropy, and we explore how the entanglement of formation and Slutsky entropy affect the synchronization coefficient in the tomogram. Our findings demonstrate that quantum synchronization can manifest in mixed states and that entanglement plays a crucial role in its emergence. Moreover, our research reveals that the slutsky entropy and entanglement of formation can drive the entomogram's evolution, and we observe that the maximum value of the slant entropy and entanglement of formation can lead to a maximum value of the synchronization coefficient. Our results also indicate that the slant entropy and entanglement of formation can be used to describe the evolution of the tomogram, and we propose that the maximum value of the synchronization coefficient can be achieved when the slant entropy and entanglement of formation are at their maximum values. Our research provides a deeper understanding of the relationship between entanglement and quantum synchronization and demonstrates that the slant entropy and entanglement of formation can be used to describe the evolution of the tomogram. Conversational agents that can adapt to various social situations and adhere to their assigned roles are crucial for developing intelligent systems capable of engaging in open-domain conversations. To achieve this, we propose a novel framework called Role Defined Conversations (RDC), which utilizes large-scale language models to create a role-specific conversation dataset. This framework enables us to generate a high-quality dataset containing over 100,000 dialogues, each adhering to a specific role and exploring a broad range of topics. We employ two evaluation methods, including human assessments and specialized benchmarks, to test the capabilities of models trained on this dataset. Our experiments demonstrate that the RDC dataset outperforms existing open-domain conversation datasets and provide insights into the characteristics of conversations influenced by defined roles.

Investigating the optimal use of resources in pest control is a complex problem that arises in various industries, including agriculture. The problem is typically modeled as a game, where the goal is to find a solution that minim costs for both the farmer and nature. A new approach to solving this problem has been achieved through the development of a specific method known as Nature's Optimal Control, which guarantees a unique and best possible outcome. The effectiveness of this approach has been demonstrated in a real-world scenario involving strawberry disease control, where the problem is modeled and a solution is found using a specific numerical technique. The study's findings suggest that this method can be applied to a broader range of control problems that involve ecological considerations.

360-degree videos offer an immersive experience, allowing viewers to navigate through a virtual environment. However, as the viewer's navigation speed and direction vary, delivering a personalized and efficient viewing experience can be challenging due to limited bandwidth. To address this challenge, we have developed a machine learning approach that predicts a user's viewport movement based on their navigation history and the video's content. A unique dataset, Virtual Travel, has been created to support this research, containing user navigation and viewport navigation data from 360-degree virtual travel videos. Our proposed method achieved a high level of accuracy in predicting user viewports, outperforming baseline methods. Additionally, we have demonstrated the effectiveness of our approach through a user study, where participants' actual viewport data matched our predicted data with a high level of similarity.

We have developed a hybrid approach to construct tensor networks that accurately represent the thermodynamic state and temporal evolution of interacting quantum systems. This approach combines the capabilities of the thermal and time-evolving variational methods with the precision of local approximations, resulting in tensor networks whose boundary conditions accurately reflect the desired thermal properties. By employing this method, we can derive compact representations of thermal density matrices following a quantum quench, and the variational nature of the approach ensures that the resulting representations are optimized for minimum energy. Furthermore, this method can be used to investigate the evolution of entanglement entropy following a quench, and we demonstrate its effectiveness by applying it to a spin chain and observing its ability to accurately capture both short and long-range correlations.

The decoupling phenomenon, where the impact of a specific factor on a system is limited under certain conditions but significant under others, is examined in relation to the limited effectiveness of the central drive in the A-type main sequence. A new approach is proposed to model limited effectiveness through restriction, and a new concept is introduced to represent systems with limited effectiveness that are independent of one another. The approach is applied to research on limited effectiveness, and the concept of scale-oriented approximation is introduced to model systems with limited effectiveness. The scale-oriented approximation is shown to be equivalent to decoupling, and the concept of scale-oriented restricted effectiveness is defined. The equivalence between scale-oriented approximation and decoupling is proven, and the concept of scale-oriented approximation is used to derive a new inequality. For a given direction $e\in\mathbb R^n$, we define the nonisotropic ball $B_e(R)$ with center at the origin and radius $R>0$ as the set of points $x\in\mathbb R^n$ such that $\max\{|x|,|xe|\}<R$. This article investigates the nonisotropic Minkowski inequality related to nonisotropic capacity $cap_e$. We establish an inequality $cap_e(B_e(1))\ge 2^{-\max\{1/p',1\}}\omega_{n-2}^{1/p'}$, where $1/p+1/p'=1$ and $\omega_{n-2}$ is the area of the $(n-2)$-dimensional unit ball. Additionally, we prove an inequality $cap_e(\lambda_1 B_{e_1})\le 2^{-\max\{1/p',1\}}\omega_{n-2}^{1/p'}\max\{\lambda_1,\lambda_1\lambda_1'\}^{1/p'}$ for any directions $e_1$ and weights $\lambda_1,\lambda_1'$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that for any ball $B(R)$ with radius $R>0$, the inequality $cap_e(B_e(R))\le R^{1/p'}\omega_{n-2}^{1/p'}$ holds.

The Microscope space mission is designed to test the weak equivalence principle (SEP) with unprecedented precision, utilizing data from the Microscope satellite. This data will be analyzed to remove the effects of satellite attitude control system (ACS) glitches on the measurement of the satellite's differential static acceleration. By applying a method to quantify the influence of these glitches, we can determine the minimum achievable accuracy of the acceleration measurement. Our study of the Microscope satellite's attitude data reveals that the noise level of the acceleration signal is primarily determined by the probability distribution of the differential angles between the satellite's test masses and the axis of the attitude control system. This analysis allows us to estimate the noise level that can be expected from the attitude control system, which is crucial for determining the minimum achievable accuracy of the acceleration measurement.

We examine a system of non-interacting, two-dimensional colloidal particles that are subject to a transverse activity gradient. This gradient causes the more active particles to migrate to the less active region, creating a macroscopic separation. The study reveals that this migration can be precisely controlled by adjusting the activity gradient and the range of particle interactions. The researchers also developed a novel theoretical model, based on an activity-dependent equation, to accurately describe the system's dynamics. This new framework provides a detailed understanding of both the transient and steady-state behaviors of the colloidal particles.

The strong shortest $k$-route cover problem on $k$ pairs within a graph $G$ involves finding the minimum edge subset $F$ such that for $k$ pairs, the shortest path between each pair in the subgraph $(G,F)$ remains unchanged from its length in $G$. This paper presents polynomial-time algorithms for determining $k$-strong shortest route covers on specific graph types, including $k$-series, $k$-parallel, and $k$-series-parallel graphs. Additionally, a heuristic is proposed to address general graphs. Computational experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach.

The color dipole gluon PDF, which is the leading contribution at small-x, is found to be zero at the next-to-leading logarithmic (NLLA) accuracy in the color dipole formalism. This paper argues that nonperturbative renormalon contributions, which are significant in the color dipole approach, cannot be disregarded in the small-x limit. By applying a Borel resummation to the perturbative series for color dipole TMD PDF, we demonstrate that an NLLA non-zero contribution emerges, which is of the same order as a certain single-gluon pole term in the backward Glauber link formalism. This finding suggests that the color dipole and GLA links may be related through a finite, non-zero shift at the NLLA accuracy.

We examine the amphibian model, a type of bipartite tree-poset partial order, and establish that its crucial density for an $n$-dimensional cube is 2 when restricted to trees, but remains an open question for forests.

We propose a novel concept called vector-sensitive magnetophotonic surface lattice, which enables the creation of chiral lattice within two-dimensional systems through a combination of periodic patterns and magnetic fields. This innovative approach allows for the generation of nonreciprocal surface photonic lattices that exhibit distinct characteristics for left- and right-handed light. By manipulating the direction of the magnetic field, we can control the topological properties of these chiral photonic bands, resulting in the formation of robust photonic pathways that are immune to backscattering. This technique offers a versatile and efficient means of generating topological photonic devices, such as waveguides and Y-junctions, that operate with high precision and minimal loss.

Zero-shot learning enables a machine to recognize new concepts without explicit training, by utilizing knowledge from related concepts. One underutilized knowledge source is information derived from a decision-based black-box framework. This framework can be used to uncover the underlying structure of a decision system, which in turn can be leveraged to recognize concepts within a decision-based black-box model. In this paper, we explore the potential of transferring knowledge from such a framework to a zero-shot learning scenario. Our initial findings indicate that this approach can successfully transfer knowledge to a zero-shot learning scenario, enabling the machine to recognize new concepts without explicit training.

The LHCb collaboration examined the decay of $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_S$ based on 3.0 fb of data collected at an integrated luminosity from $s\bar{s}$ data. The analysis was conducted using an analysis based on the decay of the $\bar{D}^0$ meson into $K^+\pi^-$, and the signal significance was found to be 6.2 standard deviations, with a signal yield of 113 $\pm$ 10 (stat) $\pm$ 11 (syst) events, and a branching fraction of $8.4 \times 10^{-4}$ $\pm$ $0.9 \times 10^{-4}$ (stat) $\pm$ $0.9 \times 10^{-4}$ (syst). Additionally, the LHCb collaboration also examined the decay of $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_S$, where the $\bar{D}^{*0}$ meson decays into $\bar{D}^0 \pi^0$, and the $\bar{D}^0$ meson is reconstructed into $K^+ \pi^-$. The signal significance was found to be 2.7 standard deviations, with a signal yield of 15 $\pm$ 10 (stat) $\pm

We present an algorithm that takes a lattice $L$ and a set $M$ as inputs, where the elements of $M$ are pairs consisting of a pair from $L$ and a pair from $M$, and produces the lattice of submodules of $M$ over a group acting on $M$, denoted as $\text{Sub}(M)$. This algorithm is effective when the group is a permutation group with a multiplicity-free action. It builds upon the method of Slutzki and Schweitzer (2019) and leverages the algorithm developed by Schweitzer (2017) for identifying maximal elements in weak order relations.

A geodetic set for a graph G is defined as a subset S where for every vertex v in G, there is at least one unique shortest path between two members of S that passes through v. The minimum size of such a subset S is referred to as the geodetic number of G. In contrast, a robust geodetic set is a subset S that satisfies a condition of distance equality for all vertices v not in S, similar to the geodetic set's condition. The minimum size of such a subset S is known as the robust geodetic number of G. This paper investigates the computational complexity of determining the robust geodetic number of a graph, focusing on specific graph classes and variations of the problem. It also presents an exact algorithm for computing the geodetic number of a graph in O(2.72^n + n^3) time.

Deep imitation learning has achieved remarkable success in real-world applications, but its success relies on high-quality expert demonstrations. When demonstrations are flawed, the problem becomes significantly more complex. To address this issue, researchers have proposed various methods, but they struggle with either computational efficiency or model performance. In this study, we introduce TRAIL, a novel approach that optimizes a loss function to balance the trade-off between these two factors. TRAIL leverages both supervised demonstrations and an agent's self-generated data to improve model performance. By leveraging a pre-trained teacher network, TRAIL is able to balance the trade-off and achieve optimal results. Our experiments demonstrate that TRAIL outperforms existing state-of-the-art approaches in balancing model performance and data efficiency.

In shared task environments, collaborative agents can learn from observing successful interactions between an expert and a human, either by following their example or by observing their guidance during a learning process with a human. This research investigates the potential of learning by observing in shared tasks and presents two primary approaches: initially, it presents a straightforward framework for learning through observation of the expert's demonstration and the human's input, utilizing basic components such as attention and reinforcement; subsequently, it presents a more advanced framework that leverages the potential of large language models to facilitate shared task learning through cooperative demonstration, demonstrating their effectiveness through comparative analysis on two shared tasks and outperforming other standalone and demonstration-based methods.

This research focuses on the measurement and calculation of two distinct error-correcting code families, namely partial asymmetric codes and parity-check asymmetric codes. We introduce efficient algorithms for computing parity-check matrices of PAC codes, alongside straightforward methods to derive their computation and storage requirements. Moreover, we develop an innovative algorithm to determine the error-correction capability of parity-check asymmetric codes, outperforming existing approaches. A key advantage of our method is its ability to handle codes with unrestricted lengths. We also provide concrete examples of error correction radii for specific PAC code instances.

Recent research has demonstrated that adding a reinforcement learning (RL) step after a translation model trained with supervised learning can enhance its performance. However, applying RL is challenging due to the large action space, which consists of all possible next tokens. In this study, we utilize a small action space that represents the next sentence rather than individual tokens. We employ PPO, a popular RL algorithm, to fine-tune a translation model that has been pre-trained with supervised learning. To overcome data scarcity for training, we develop a reinforcement learning step that mimics human preferences based on the scores assigned by a scoring model. Experiments conducted on the IWSLT 2017 German-to-English and WMT 2018 English-to-German datasets show that our method yields significant improvements over the baseline models. Notably, the proposed approach achieves a substantial gain of +1.01 on the German-to-English dataset, whereas direct RL training is not feasible due to the lack of sufficient data.

This research paper proposes a novel calibration method for a robot depth camera system, enabling accurate end-effector position estimation. Unlike conventional approaches, our method uniquely tackles the challenge of calibrating and tracking the camera without any pre-marked features on the robot end-effector. We employ a neural network to predict the camera's orientation and a novel loss function to guide it towards optimal calibration. Notably, our approach eliminates the need for manual calibration and can be performed in an unmarked, uncontrolled environment. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method.

This study focuses on the unique properties of the Quark Flavor Symmetry region within the quenching transition. Specifically, we investigate how the QFS boundary influences the formation of a quark-gluon plasma, a hadron-quark mixed state, and a hadronizing matter. Our findings indicate that the QFS region is a stable, separate state from the quark-gluon plasma and hadronizing matter, yet it can coexist with a hadron-quark mixed state under certain conditions. We also observe that a mixed state with the QFS region can exist at a higher temperature than a mixed state without the QFS region. Furthermore, we find that an initial quark matter state can persist until the mixed state with the QFS region reaches a critical temperature, at which point a quark-gluon plasma is formed. These insights can be tested through heavy-ion collision experiments.

Research on social media and online forums has revealed significant correlations between individuals' expressed opinions and their political leanings. However, there is limited knowledge regarding the political preferences of people based on their consumption of digital news. This study aims to bridge this gap by analyzing the political ideology of 10,000 American adults, based on the news sources they read. Our research utilizes the AllSides ideological bias scale to assess the political bias of 1000 news sources and employs a consumption matrix to model the ideological bias of individual consumers. The sources' biases are strongly correlated with those of their audience, and our findings suggest that the sources' AllSides ratings are a reliable predictor of consumer ideology. Furthermore, the sources consumed by liberals are more distinct from those consumed by conservatives than they are from those consumed by moderates. This research also highlights the importance of considering the political biases of news sources when making recommendations for personalized news recommendations.

We provide an overview of the current knowledge concerning the irreducible word length in the standard generating set of the Thompson group V. A key feature of this length is that it can take on values that are not achievable by any other element in the group. As a consequence, there exists a finite set of expressions using the group's generating symbols that cannot be simplified to represent the same group element as any other expression of equal or shorter length.

This paper presents both experimental and theoretical findings on a two-level quantum system, specifically a superconducting qubit, that has reached a steady state out of equilibrium under periodic driving. In our setup, the qubit is isolated from its environment using a tunable resonator, allowing it to reach this equilibrium driven state even when connected to a heat bath. As a result, the qubit's population and coherence stabilize at fixed values, while the surrounding environment experiences a stationary nonequilibrium state characterized by a steady-state density matrix. Our experimental data aligns closely with the predictions made by our theoretical model based on a time-dependent rate equation. This study provides a platform for observing phenomena such as interference effects and coherence in the surrounding environment as a consequence of the qubit's steady, nonequilibrium state.

Various researchers have extensively studied higher-order submanifold geometry, particularly biharmonic hypersurfaces in relation to various differential operators in Euclidean space. This study focuses on characterizing and classifying the biharmonic hypersurfaces in the Euclidean space when influenced by the skew-symmetric operator Delta plus nabla squared. We provide a comprehensive list of the required conditions for such hypersurfaces. Additionally, numerous examples have been provided to further illustrate the obtained results.

Given a collectible item x, we say a set K is p/q-identifiable id if for every possible outcome, the probability of x being in K is consistently p/q and no other value. We investigate the existence of a collectible collection K consisting of all possible outcomes, where K is p/q-identifiable id and has the maximum possible size.

We propose a new theory called axion-still-neutrino shadow matter, which is based on the idea of supersymmetry. In this theory, the neutralinos are held together by gravity to form a galactic halo, and they remain stationary due to their minimal velocity within the galaxy. The theory posits that the mass of neutralinos is extremely high, which allows them to interact with each other through axion emission and thus maintain their stability. The mass of neutralinos is calculated to be between $10^{12}$ and $10^{14}$ GeV, which is consistent with recent observations of the gamma-ray spectrum from the Galactic Center.

The LAMOST time-domain exploration (TDE) survey is set to revolutionize our understanding of stellar variability and transient phenomena on a grand scale. The LAMOST telescope will conduct repeated observations of 40 million targets over the course of 5 years, with each target being monitored 10 times per year, with 8 observations per night, spaced 15 minutes apart. The $K_2$ plates, originally used in the Kepler and K2 space telescopes' missions, are being employed by LAMOST to carry out this survey. The LAMOST TDE survey will cover a vast area of the sky, from the galactic center to the outer reaches, with a magnitude limit of 9, encompassing a wide range of stellar populations. The LAMOST TDE survey will be able to detect a wide range of transient phenomena, including variables that are difficult to observe with the Kepler and K2 missions, such as AGNs, pulsars, and magnetars. The LAMOST TDE survey will be able to detect a wide range of variables, including RR Lyrae stars, Cepheids, and white dwarfs, with a period variability that is difficult to observe with the Kepler and K2 missions. This study introduces an innovative approach to three-dimensional semantic segmentation of clinical images, specifically focusing on T1-weighted MRI images used for brain tumor identification and removal. To address the varying importance of image regions, we developed an edge-gated three-dimensional convolutional neural network. This novel architecture combines precise edge detection with a sophisticated gating mechanism to prioritize critical tumor boundaries. Experimental results demonstrate that the edge-gated network outperforms traditional methods, achieving a significant improvement in Dice score by 10% in comparison to a baseline three-dimensional semantic segmentation approach.

MongoDB is a popular NoSQL database that offers high scalability and flexibility, but lacks robust data consistency and reliability features. To address this, we developed a transactional integrity validator for MongoDB, which is a transactional protocol that guarantees data consistency and reliability. Our validator was benchmarked against a range of workloads and demonstrated a 100% success rate in maintaining transactional integrity, with only a 1.5x performance overhead. Our results suggest that our validator can be used to enhance the reliability of MongoDB applications without compromising their efficiency.

A recent study by the author, Lee, in 2019 established the $e$-positivity of the chromatic symmetric polynomials for convex polyominoes. This paper extends that finding to a broader category of shapes called nonseparating unions of convex polyominoes. The $e$-positivity property for these more complex figures is demonstrated using an innovative new combinatorial approach, specifically an inverse shadowing technique applied to the Kostka tableau.

This research paper delves into the concepts of renaming and insight discovery through a fresh perspective, known as the Hindsight Summarization (HiS) metric. By applying HiS, we've uncovered a renaming technique called Executive Function (EF), which leverages function points to identify and rename high-value functions within a codebase. We've also integrated EF into a code evolution framework, resulting in a more effective and maintainable codebase. Furthermore, EF's high information gain enables it to outperform existing techniques in various scenarios. Additionally, we've introduced a new method, called HiS-Mutation (HiSM), which combines function inheritance and high-value function renaming to generate more realistic and effective code mutations. We've also incorporated a mutation strategy, known as Executive Function Mutation (EFM), which leverages high information gain and high HiS to create more effective mutations. Our findings demonstrate that our proposed techniques outperform existing methods in multiple experiments.

The quality of deep learning models for medical image analysis is heavily influenced by biases present in training datasets. These biases, often referred to as intrinsic prejudice, are difficult to identify and remove. This study proposes a novel approach to detect such biases automatically without requiring additional information about the data. By using a method that involves comparing the output of a medical image collection's neural network to its corresponding label, we can identify and quantify the prejudice present in the dataset. This approach is demonstrated on two medical image collections, showing that our proposed method can effectively detect biases present in the datasets.

A complex system's hidden structure and behavior can be studied through spin reversal dynamics in triangularly connected metallic nanoassemblies. These assemblies, characterized by a combination of nearest-neighbor and triangular interactions, were simulated using a classical Heisenberg model. The study revealed that the nature of the spin reversal dynamics is influenced by the ratio of triangular interaction strength to nearest-neighbor interaction strength. Notably, a distinct change in the universal scaling behavior was observed at a specific threshold, indicating the presence of a concealed geometric arrangement within the assembly. This discovery highlights the potential for uncovering underlying patterns in intricate systems by analyzing their underlying geometric and scaling properties.

A phenomenon known as solar breeze occurs at the Sun's surface, where energy is transferred from the Sun to the Earth through electromagnetic fields, ultimately influencing the planet's climate. To better understand this process, a sophisticated system of models is being developed to analyze data collected by the Parker Solar Probe as it approaches the probe's perihelion, just 9.86 million kilometers from the Sun. The probe's advanced magnetic field and plasma field instruments are providing valuable insights into the solar breeze's properties, including the behavior of electrons and ions, and how they are affected by the probe's orientation and the solar breeze's overall structure. These findings are being analyzed to refine models of energy transfer and to predict the impact of solar activity on the Earth's climate.

Speech-emotion recognition is a significant task in speech technology that is hindered by data scarcity and the difficulty of collecting labeled data. Self-learning approaches using deep reinforcement learning (DL) have been explored to mitigate this limitation, but they are susceptible to the accumulation of incorrect labels due to their lack of global optimality. In this study, we introduce a speech-emotion recognition framework that combines domain adaptation and deep reinforcement learning (DL). Initially, a supervised neural network is trained on a limited set of data, and then it is fine-tuned using a deep reinforcement learning agent. The baseline domain adaptation approach and the DL's mean squared error loss function guide the model to minimize discrepancies between predicted and actual outputs, thereby preventing the model from learning incorrect information. We conducted comprehensive experiments on the SAVE and SAVE-M datasets, and the results demonstrate that our proposed method outperforms existing approaches in terms of accuracy and robustness.

We studied the structural and magnetic properties of Bi5FeTi3O15 in four layers across a range of pressures (0-6.5 GPa) using nuclear diffraction techniques. Our findings show that Bi5FeTi3O15 undergoes two phase transitions at 2.5 GPa and 5.5 GPa, with the high-pressure phases reverting to the original state upon releasing pressure. Neutron diffraction data indicate that Bi5FeTi3O15 experiences changes in magnetic ordering with elevated pressure, with the initial high-spin state of Fe3+ (4.5 $\mu_B$) at 0 GPa shifting to an intermediate-spin state (2.5 $\mu_B$) at 6.5 GPa.

This research paper focuses on the development of numerical methods to solve the discrete-continuous shortest path problem, with a specific application to optimizing flight paths. A novel approach is proposed to generate high-quality initial solutions for the optimization problem, with a view to improving the efficiency of solving this problem. The effectiveness of the proposed method is demonstrated through a case study involving the optimization of flight paths between two points in a given airspace. The results show significant improvements in flight time and fuel consumption, with the approach showing potential for broader application in the design of optimal trajectories.

This research examines a robust shock wave within a cosmological model that is expanding uniformly, specifically within a spherical region. The shock wave's influence persists despite the chaotic fluctuations inherent to the system. The study also compares the behavior of the shock wave within the cosmological context to that within a closed system. The model's parameters can be manipulated to mimic the behavior of a Type Ia supernova, and the relationship between the size of the cavity and the location of the maximum brightness within the shock wave is explored.

A new class of Schrödinger operators is identified, characterized by smooth, continuous potential functions without bound states, and eigenfunctions that are polynomials of the form $x_n P_{n-1}(x)$. These operators are described analytically using the theory of isomonodromic deformations. Within this framework, the polynomials $P_n(x)$ are shown to be a broader version of the classical Hermite polynomials, with the property of being "quasi-orthogonal" with respect to a weight function that exhibits first-order poles at specific points. Additionally, the relationship between these particles-on-the-line models and the theory of exceptional orthogonal polynomials is explored.

The process of peeling off a sticky strip from a surface produces an unpredictable, intermittent sound. This sound is linked to the sudden release of non-sticking parts as they break free from the adhesive points. This phenomenon serves as an excellent model for studying phase transitions in adhesive processes. In this study, a novel method is proposed to analyze the intermittent nature of the sound by utilizing a time-scale parameter to categorize distinct sound states. This approach provides valuable insights into the hidden relationships within the dynamic system and the evolution of its arrangement over time.

Our theoretical analysis indicates that planar Josephson junctions and small SQUIDs do not exhibit the vortex phase, instead remaining in a state where no vortices are present. This outcome is in contrast to previously observed experiments and theories which suggested the occurrence of a distinct, vortex-rich, intermediate state between the resistive and superconducting states.

This research provides a closed-form solution for pricing options under dynamic delta hedging, where account collateral is subject to a cost due to trading expenses. The solution is derived by modifying the standard Black-Scholes equation to account for option delta and the cost of trading the underlying asset. The option's price is then determined by solving this modified equation, with the option's delta playing a crucial role in the solution. The solution is also used to estimate the option's gamma, which is an essential metric for option traders. The model is validated through Monte Carlo simulations, which show that the option's gamma is significantly impacted by the account collateral cost, with the effect being more pronounced for options with shorter expiration dates and higher volatility. The research has implications for option traders, who can use the model to better understand the impact of account collateral on option pricing and risk management.

This research examines the effective properties of a specific type of contrast composite material, where one component has an extremely high contrast and is isolated from the other component by a thin boundary layer. The study analyzes how the material's properties behave under the influence of scale interactions when subjected to differential constraints, such as the Kirchhoff plate model. The results indicate that the limiting material's behavior is heavily influenced by the balance between three key factors: the elevated contrast, the differential material's mode, and the small boundary layer. The research provides the precise relationships between these parameters that yield distinct, non-degenerate limits. The material's response is also explored through the use of explicit example constructions, particularly for the Kirchhoff plate model.

This research paper examines the optimal allocation of a risky investment prospect in a dynamic model that considers intergenerational social mobility. The model's framework is expanded to consider the transferability of risky assets across generations, which is then used to determine the conditions under which it is optimal to transfer the prospect to a new investor. The research also reveals how the transferability of risk influences the distribution of risk across the economy, as well as the factors that affect the probability of transferring the prospect. The results indicate that the transfer of the prospect is more likely to occur when the underlying asset exhibits high volatility, the economy shows high mobility, and the investor has a high degree of risk aversion. The research paper's findings are further illustrated through numerical examples and potential applications are discussed.

This paper provides a comprehensive overview of the cutting-edge developments in high-power solid-state laser technology. It covers key areas such as pump diode and laser diode bar advancements, improvements in laser crystal and glass components, and the progress made in fiber lasers. The presentation of this topic is tailored to researchers and practitioners in the field of high-power laser systems.

We establish a nonlinear dimension reduction theorem for subsets of $\ell_p$ spaces, where the dimension reduction magnitude is proportional to a given small value $\varepsilon$. This theorem provides a mapping from a given closed, incompressible subset of an $\ell_p$ space to a corresponding subset of an $\ell_{p'}$ space of significantly lower dimension, maintaining a nearly $\varepsilon$-isometric relationship. This holds true for all $p$ values, excluding the interval $(4,\infty)$, and for space dimensions up to three.

A novel approach to beam characterization, specifically through brightness scans, is introduced. These scans can be effectively utilized to determine key parameters such as transverse profile, emittance, and brightness. The proposed method is illustrated with a case study on a high-intensity proton beam at the CERN PS, demonstrating that even with limited measurement data, the transverse profile can be accurately reconstructed. The scan's efficiency is enhanced by utilizing a fast-tuning mechanism, reducing the beam intensity, and employing a large acceptance diagnostic device. The method is also applicable to other contexts, including high-intensity beams and those with complex structures.

This paper introduces a distributed subgradient technique that enables honest participants to outperform any malicious attacker in a network environment, where the attacker can control one node and has access to unlimited information. By implementing this method on multiple nodes, the attacker's advantage is negated, and the system achieves an optimal rate of convergence, matching the theoretical limit of $O(1/\sqrt{T})$. We also develop a quantized version of this technique that operates effectively even with limited data transmission capacity.

We have developed a Python library called s4cmb to replicate the data generation process of various instruments that have measured the cosmic microwave background (CMB) and produced catalogs of galaxies. This library enables researchers to generate simulated data for multiple instruments simultaneously, incorporating realistic characteristics such as beam shapes, frequency distributions, and levels of instrumental noise. By doing so, s4cmb facilitates the development and testing of new analysis techniques within a unified framework, which can be applied to multiple datasets. The library is designed to be modular and can be extended to include additional simulations of other instruments or simulated data sets. Furthermore, s4cmb is being used in conjunction with the public s4 and s3-2 datasets, and its source code is available on GitHub for others to access and contribute to.

NLP models trained on large datasets have shown remarkable performance in various tasks, including word arrangement. To investigate their underlying mechanisms, we examined the pre-trained BART model's ability to solve the "least-squares word arrangement" problem. Our research revealed that solving this problem is a complex task that requires solving multiple sub-tasks, such as word relationship learning and semantic understanding. To address this issue, we proposed a new dataset and a baseline model that leverages the hierarchical structure of sentences to solve the problem. Our results indicate that our proposed model outperformed the BART model and other baselines, suggesting that word arrangement problems should be considered in future evaluations of NLP models.

Deepfakes are a type of fraudulent media that uses artificial intelligence to create deceptive and realistic-looking fake content. They pose a significant threat to individuals and society as a whole. Deepfake detection is the process of identifying and detecting these fraudulent media. Deep neural networks are commonly used for this purpose, but they have several limitations, including the fact that they are computationally expensive, require a large amount of data, and are prone to overfitting. In this paper, we propose a novel deep learning architecture called the MD-CSDNetwork, which is designed to overcome these limitations. The MD-CSDNetwork is a cross-sewn network that is composed of two sub-networks, which are designed to process different types of features and fuse them to generate a more accurate output. The MD-CSDNetwork is shown to achieve superior performance on several widely used deepfake detection benchmarks, outperforming state-of-the-art methods.

A novel LDPC code structure has been proposed, which is based on a dual-layered, binary, degree-degree distributed channel. This new construction overcomes a previous limitation identified by Richardson and Urbanke, who found that any single binary degree-degree graph is susceptible to errors under certain conditions.

A novel, secure method for implementing the quantum key distribution with a new attack-resistant technique called "decoy-state" has been widely adopted, especially when utilizing laser light. This innovation was introduced to address the limitations imposed by laser light in QKD systems. This study investigates a new, secure method for executing the Decoy-State protocol by introducing a randomization technique on the photon's phase, demonstrating that a specific attack, previously thought to compromise the system, can be mitigated through this approach. Furthermore, this randomization method allows for a broader range of compatible keys to be allocated, increasing the system's overall efficiency. Our research provides theoretical calculations and simulations to support these findings, offering valuable insights for designing more efficient and secure quantum systems.

In 1923, Menger developed a general framework for Minkowski's work on the geometry of angles. Building on this foundation, we provide a revised resolution to two longstanding problems that Menger believed were related to the geometry of angle spaces. Furthermore, we present our own interpretation of these issues, along with a fresh approach to addressing them. Our solution not only confirms the original conclusions but also broadens the scope of the original theorem. Additionally, we establish a direct equivalence between Minkowski's angle geometry and a specific type of metric geometry.

This paper explores the statistical behavior of successive minima of the Minkowski rank lattice within number fields, specifically focusing on how this behavior relates to geometric invariants of curves under the action of subfields. By employing techniques from the geometry of numbers, we derive bounds on successive minima and utilize these to analyze the distribution of rank lattice points. We then apply these findings to investigate the distribution of points in $SL_n(\mathcal{O}_F)$-orbits of $X$, where $X$ is a homogeneous space over a number field $F$. We also discuss the implications of our results on the distribution of points in curves and their invariants.

A novel approach to measuring gas temperature, pressure, and specific components has been demonstrated using femtosecond-picosecond hybrid terahertz rotational coherent anti-Stokes Raman scattering. This method was successfully executed with a dual-laser probe system, combining femtosecond and picosecond lasers. The study focused on air as the target gas, and the use of a femtosecond laser for generating the THz field and a picosecond laser for detecting the rotational response was shown to minimize the required femtosecond laser energy. As a result, the spatial resolution of the measurement system was significantly improved. The study also highlighted the use of a machine learning-based data processing method, which allowed for the simultaneous estimation of multiple gas parameters from a single type of measurement data. The results indicate that the proposed hybrid measurement system can accurately evaluate temperature, pressure, and the oxygen-to-nitrogen ratio in a single-shot manner, with a maximum error of 1.5K, 0.01atm, and 0.05, respectively.

This research paper proves that the quantum cluster algebra $\mathcal{A}_R(q\hbar,\mathcal{X})$ associated with any skew-group type quantum cluster pattern is isomorphic to a specific quantum algebra $R\langle\langle\mathcal{L}|\mathcal{R}\rangle\rangle$ defined by its generators and relations. Furthermore, the relation between the set of generators $\mathcal{L}$ and the set of relations $\mathcal{R}$ can be expressed using quantum Plucker relations. Consequently, the quantum cluster algebra is also isomorphic to another equivalent algebra $\mathcal{A}'_R(q\hbar,\mathcal{L},\mathcal{R})$. By establishing the relationship between the Plucker relations and the quantum Grassmannian, the paper provides a parametric quantum Plucker decomposition for the Grassmannian $G(k,n)$, where $k<n/2$.

In decentralized learning scenarios, a significant number of malicious nodes can intentionally send false data to a large number of honest nodes, leading to a situation where the graph of communication between the honest nodes is divided into multiple separate components. This paper presents an innovative approach to addressing this challenge by proposing a new algorithm called DR-DSGD, which is based on a distributionally robust optimization framework. This new method guarantees that the final model it produces will be within a guaranteed distance of the optimal model that could be produced by an ideal centralized algorithm, given the same data. Numerical experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of DR-DSGD in scenarios with a large number of malicious nodes. The method's performance can be further improved by adjusting the level of robustness to the influence of the malicious nodes.

The development of computer simulations for magnetic storage systems has been so impactful that it has significantly impacted their real-world design. Initially, these simulations were first created in the 1960s, and they were initially used to validate the functionality of new read/write heads and recording media. Since then, computer simulations have been increasingly used to optimize the performance of storage systems and they have been used to balance the conflicting demands of capacity and speed. This paper provides an in-depth review of the development of computer simulations for magnetic storage systems, and it also outlines the fundamental principles behind these simulations and the key components that are typically included in modern simulations.

We conclude that a Bayesian approach is a useful tool for analyzing the impact of various uncertainties on the generated medium-modified jets and can be used to interpret the data from the LHC.

Cryptocurrencies were initially created to circumvent traditional financial systems, yet their primary use has been for money laundering and fraud. One of the largest cryptocurrency scams ever discovered, Forsage, operated through a multi-level marketing scheme embedded in a blockchain smart contract. The Forsage scam defrauded over 100,000 victims of more than $400 million, with the code being publicly accessible for analysis. This research paper dissects the code and business model of Forsage, providing a detailed examination of its structure and offering insights into the future of fraud through cryptocurrency and blockchain technology.

To address the lack of quark effects in standard Drell-Yan analyses, a new approach is proposed that incorporates these effects through a new set of distribution amplitudes. This new approach is applicable to a broad range of Drell-Yan processes, with the process $ep\to \gamma^*p_e$ serving as an example. By applying the Substantial Quark Effect (SQE) formalism to this process, we derive an exact expression for the cross-section, which incorporates the impact of finite quark size effects on the distribution of quarks within the proton. This new approach also allows for the factorization of the SQE distribution into universal components, which can be experimentally measured. By applying this new approach to this process, we can extract the SQE distribution and gain insight into the behavior of quarks within the proton.

The accuracy of time-dependent density functional theory within the adiabatic approximation is compromised by the omission of non-adiabatic atomic nucleus motion. This limitation can be mitigated by utilizing a minimal tight-binding model with a two-band structure, which simplifies the problem while retaining essential physics. In this study, we demonstrate the ability to derive such a model from density functional theory, and further show that the resulting theory's validity is ensured by the invariance of atomic nucleus interactions to the specific parameterization of the tight-binding Hamiltonian. This insight facilitates the systematic development of reliable tight-binding models with two-band structures.

The AdS/MERA correspondence suggests that holographic error correction can be achieved using tensor network representations, specifically through the Haah's harmonic code, which is a topologically non-trivial code. To adapt this to more realistic settings, we propose a modified version of the MERA network, called the Hierarchical Mirror Network, that mirrors the structure of the harmonic code. This network is then mirrored by adding swap gates to create a hierarchical code that is equivalent to the Haah's code. As a result, the code's minimum distance and error correction capabilities are determined by the logarithm of the system size, which is a property shared with the harmonic code. Furthermore, we show that a non-logarithmic scaling can be attained by altering the network's hierarchical scaling factor, thus providing a flexible framework for approximating topological Hamiltonians and codes with long-range harmonic potentials.

A computational model of retinal chromophores, which are responsible for human vision, is examined in a modified state where they continuously change form when exposed to light. This model retinal chromophore demonstrates efficient photoisomerization even as it reaches a stable, continuous state. By analyzing the system's response to varying light frequencies, we find an unexpected phenomenon where the system's susceptibility to parametric changes reaches an extreme value. This extreme susceptibility arises from a rare, high-energy state that is formed from a combination of very low and very high vibrational states. The system's behavior in this extreme state is influenced by a balance between the chromophore's internal energy and its interaction with the surrounding environment. The findings suggest that this extreme susceptibility may play a crucial role in vision, as retinal chromophores are subject to constant vibrational energy from surrounding molecules. The research also suggests that this phenomenon may be relevant to other biomolecules that rely on retinal chromophores for their function.

Deep-learning models have achieved remarkable success in various domains, including image and speech recognition, as well as time-series analysis. Despite their effectiveness, the underlying mechanisms of these models remain somewhat opaque, hindering their ability to be easily interpreted. This research seeks to address this limitation by introducing a deep-learning framework capable of not only predicting outcomes but also offering insights into process performance through process mining applications. By combining a data-driven approach to reconstructing process flows with the predictive capabilities of deep neural networks, this proposed method leverages process variants to enhance predictive performance. The results demonstrate significant improvements over traditional machine-learning techniques, with notable reductions in prediction errors. Additionally, the study highlights the value of incorporating model interpretability, offering a more comprehensive understanding of the models' predictions.

Social networks provide valuable insights into human behavior, which can be particularly useful during crises. During events like earthquakes, people's thoughts and feelings are often expressed freely on Twitter, offering a unique opportunity to analyze how individuals cope with sudden disasters. This paper aims to investigate the 2020 Izmir earthquake's impact on Twitter users, both locally and globally, by examining posts made in Turkish and English. By applying text mining techniques, we identified key topics discussed and differences in language use between the two language groups. Our findings reveal that while the main topics remained similar, there were notable differences in sentiment and coping mechanisms expressed in Turkish and English. This research contributes to our understanding of how people respond to sudden disasters on Twitter and suggests potential avenues for future study.

This non-ordinary nature is crucial in proving that certain Toeplitz operators on holomorphic Sobolev spaces possess only scalar spectra.

This research focuses on the PT-symmetric point in a finite periodic waveguide system, taking into account its ability to transmit waves and maintain bidirectional clarity. A finite periodic PT-symmetric network is analyzed, and the conditions for achieving the PT-symmetric point in terms of transmission and bidirectional clarity are derived. A method to control the transition from the exceptional point to a regular point in a finite periodic PT-symmetric network is also presented. A model based on a finite periodic PT-symmetric network is proposed to achieve the coherent flawless absorption-lasing point, a critical point in the spectrum of a finite periodic PT-symmetric network, and its realization is demonstrated experimentally.

The current approach to analyzing sparse random networks relies heavily on pairwise node independence, which fails to account for the intricate web of interdependencies that can arise among network nodes. We propose a novel statistical framework that extends beyond this limitation by employing a stochastic framework to model the emergence of complex connections between nodes based on threshold-based criteria. This framework enables us to investigate the dynamics of Threshhold Auto-Logica (TAL) networks, where multiple nodes can interact with each other through logic gates. Through an entropy minimization approach, we derive a general equation for the time evolution of TAL networks and identify conditions under which the system reaches a stable state. Our numerical simulations reveal that, in contrast to Standard Random Networks (SRNs), TAL networks exhibit unique temporal patterns, including oscillations and chaos, which are influenced by the complexity of the logic gates used. Notably, our framework enables the exploration of intricate dynamics that were previously unattainable in studies of Standard Random Networks.

This paper provides explicit analytical formulas for calculating matrix elements of single-particle and particle-particle/particle-hole operators between any two Hartree-Fock-Bogoliubov states. These states are defined by their respective quasiparticle configurations, and the analysis takes into consideration the non-orthogonal nature of the underlying wave functions. Such detailed expressions are valuable tools for researchers in nuclear structure physics, especially when utilizing the HFB method in its various forms.

The use of point clouds in 3D object detection and tracking has gained popularity due to their ease of acquisition and cost-effectiveness. However, their irregular nature poses challenges for effective feature extraction. While various methods have been proposed to address this challenge, they often suffer from high computational costs and limited scalability. In this paper, we propose a novel approach called TPC, a simple yet effective point cloud representation that is robust to geometric transformations. Our method employs a lightweight and efficient strategy to convert point clouds into a voxel grid, which is then used to extract features. Our approach is particularly suited for real-time applications due to its low computational costs and high scalability. Our method has been shown to outperform state-of-the-art approaches on multiple benchmarks, including the KITTI and SUNRGBD datasets. Our code is available at https://github.com/zhengzheng99/TPC.

throughput as a function of the number of radar users and the duration of
